extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, counsel, and parties in USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: An Administrative Law Judge initial decision applying USPTO disciplinary rules to alleged misconduct by a registered patent practitioner, including findings, conclusions of law, and sanctions. It explains procedural requirements (service, answers, default), substantive rule violations, standards for proof, and factors for imposing sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory and regulatory basis for USPTO discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO has exclusive authority to establish qualifications for admission and to suspend or exclude persons from practice before it under 35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(D) and to discipline practitioners under 35 U.S.C. § 32. Disciplinary hearings are conducted under 37 C.F.R. Part 11, Subpart C, and Section 7 of the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 556.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that practitioner must receive notice and an opportunity for a hearing before discipline; cites Kroll v. Finnerty; identifies the hearing officer authority (HUD ALJs appointed). Use these statutes/regulations as the foundation for jurisdiction and procedurally required protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof in OED disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving any alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence, per 37 C.F.R. § 11.49.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This governs the standard for establishing violations. The decision applies the clear-and-convincing standard in evaluating alleged misconduct and cites prior USPTO precedents that applied the same standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default judgment rule for failure to answer (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to timely file an answer to a disciplinary complaint will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in entry of default judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tribunal treats an unanswered complaint as admitted facts; cites multiple USPTO initial decisions granting default judgment where respondents failed to answer (e.g., In re Whitney, Morishita, Schwedler). Practical note: timely filing an answer or showing good cause is necessary to avoid default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner contact-information duties (37 C.F.R. § 11.11(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Registered patent practitioners must notify the OED Director of the postal address for their office, at least one and up to three email addresses where they receive email, and a business telephone number, and must notify of every change to each within thirty days of the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to determine proper service and to assess compliance with investigatory requests. The decision documents returned mail and undelivered emails as evidence that the practitioner failed to maintain up‑to‑date contact information, which affected the investigation and service attempts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of failing diligence include: not submitting client-paid filing fees to the USPTO, allowing an application to become abandoned, failing to file petitions to revive, and failing to inform a client promptly and adequately about limitations on ability or willingness to handle a matter. Decision cites USPTO precedent where similar conduct violated § 11.103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client communications (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3), (a)(4), (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must keep clients reasonably informed about the status of a matter, comply with reasonable requests for information, and explain a matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied where respondent repeatedly failed to respond to client inquiries about application status, failed to disclose abandonment or options to revive, and provided inaccurate or misleading status information. Prior decisions cited for guidance on what constitutes inadequate communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safekeeping property / handling client funds (37 C.F.R. § 11.115(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must promptly deliver funds that a client is entitled to receive and appropriately handle client funds and property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to remit a client's patent filing fees to the USPTO and failure to refund client payments constitute violations. Decision cites prior cases where not returning unearned fees or failing to remit funds was an aggravating factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties after termination / protecting client interests (37 C.F.R. § 11.116(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon termination of representation, a practitioner must take steps to the extent reasonably practicable to protect a client’s interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes returning unearned fees, transferring files, notifying the client and relevant authorities, and otherwise preserving client rights. The Tribunal found a de facto termination where practitioner ceased communication and did not protect client interests; cites precedent where similar conduct violated § 11.116(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: knowingly giving false reasons for not receiving Office notices, repeatedly representing an intent to file a petition to revive when not intending to do so, and soliciting and accepting client filing fees yet never submitting them to the USPTO. Such conduct supports findings of dishonesty and is cited as aggravating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and significance of mental state, especially knowing conduct (37 C.F.R. § 11.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Knowingly, known, or knows' means actual knowledge of the fact in question; a person’s knowledge may be inferred from circumstances. The mental state (intentional, knowing, or negligent) affects the degree of discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing conduct occurs when a practitioner acts with conscious awareness of the nature or circumstances of the conduct. The Tribunal assesses whether misconduct was negligent, knowing, or intentional, noting that knowing or intentional misconduct warrants more severe discipline than negligence. Cites case law and STANDARDS § 3.0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Four factors guide sanctions: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client/public/legal system/profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused; and (4) the existence of aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal applies these factors, relying on ABA ANNOTATED STANDARDS FOR IMPOSING LAWYER SANCTIONS and USPTO precedent to determine appropriate discipline. Decision describes how each factor was evaluated in the case (e.g., duty violated, knowing conduct, actual and potential harm, multiple aggravators, one mitigator).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors (ABA STANDARDS § 9.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating circumstances (if present) may justify more severe sanctions; the STANDARDS identify eleven aggravating factors (e.g., dishonest or selfish motive; pattern of misconduct; multiple offenses; bad faith obstruction; refusal to acknowledge wrongdoing; substantial experience; indifference to restitution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tribunal identified seven applicable aggravating factors in this case and explains each: dishonest/selfish motive (collecting fees and not remitting them), pattern of misconduct (repeated failures to inform client and cooperate), multiple offenses (violations of several USPTO Rules), bad-faith obstruction (failure to participate in disciplinary process), refusal to acknowledge wrongdoing (no remorse), substantial experience in practice (decades of patent practice), and indifference to making restitution (no refund). Prior decisions and authorities cited for each aggravator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors (ABA STANDARDS § 9.3 et seq.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigating circumstances may justify reduced discipline; the STANDARDS list possible mitigators such as absence of prior disciplinary record, remorse, cooperation, and timely good-faith efforts to make restitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tribunal found one mitigating factor applicable here: absence of prior disciplinary record (STANDARDS § 9.32(a)). The decision notes that this factor is significant but outweighed by multiple aggravators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of USPTO precedents and ABA Standards in evaluation and sanctioning
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal relies on prior USPTO decisions and the ABA ANNOTATED STANDARDS FOR IMPOSING LAWYER SANCTIONS to interpret rules, identify aggravating/mitigating factors, and select appropriate sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites multiple prior USPTO decisions (e.g., In re Crosby, Vieira, Hamill, Flindt, Fuess, Stecewycz) as comparable examples for findings and sanctions; indicates that consistency with precedent informs sanction selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribunal authority to impose sanctions (37 C.F.R. § 11.20)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal (hearing officer) has broad authority to impose appropriate disciplinary sanctions under USPTO regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision explains that the Tribunal may suspend, exclude, impose probationary terms, and condition reinstatement on restitution or other requirements, citing § 11.20 and prior decisions for scope of remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties while suspended (37 C.F.R. § 11.58)
rubrics_metrics.description: A suspended practitioner is subject to duties set forth in 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 while suspended from practice before the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision orders suspension and directs respondent to § 11.58 for the specific duties (the decision does not recite the full duties but makes compliance a condition of the suspension and reinstatement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal rights and finality (37 C.F.R. § 11.55(a); § 11.54(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Either party may appeal an initial decision to the USPTO Director by filing a notice of appeal within fourteen (14) days of the date of the initial decision; in the absence of appeal, the decision becomes the final decision of the USPTO Director pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides timeline and mechanism for appeal; practical consequence that failing to appeal finalizes the sanctions.
